q: A vaccine protects a person against a disease mainly by:
o: Supplying ready-made antibodies from another person
Killing every microorganism already in the body
Replacing the person's damaged white blood cells
Stimulating the body to make antibodies and memory cells
x: A vaccine carries antigens that trigger the person's own immune response, producing antibodies and long-lived memory cells. Ready-made antibodies give passive immunity, which is not how a vaccine works.

q: The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is produced commercially by inserting a viral gene into:
o: Yeast cells
Human liver cells
Tobacco mosaic virus
Penicillium mould
x: The gene for the hepatitis B surface protein is placed in yeast, which grows quickly and makes the protein in large amounts. The protein is then purified and used as the vaccine.

q: The active ingredient of the recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is:
o: The whole live hepatitis B virus
The surface antigen protein of the virus
The heat-killed whole hepatitis B virus
The complete viral DNA genome
x: Only the viral surface antigen (HBsAg) made by genetically engineered yeast is used. It contains no viral nucleic acid, so it cannot cause infection.

q: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
o: Injected (Salk) polio vaccine
Tetanus toxoid
Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine
Oral (Sabin) polio vaccine
x: The oral Sabin polio vaccine contains live but weakened poliovirus. The Salk vaccine contains killed virus, tetanus toxoid is an inactivated toxin, and the hepatitis B vaccine is a single recombinant protein.

q: The injected Salk polio vaccine is an example of a vaccine made from:
o: Live weakened virus
A single recombinant viral protein
An inactivated bacterial toxin
Killed (inactivated) virus
x: Salk's vaccine uses poliovirus inactivated with chemicals such as formaldehyde, so the virus cannot multiply. The oral Sabin vaccine, by contrast, uses live attenuated virus.

q: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided in people with a seriously weakened immune system because:
o: The weakened organism can still multiply and may cause disease in them
They contain no antigens that the body can recognise
They are destroyed by stomach acid before acting
They produce only passive immunity in such people
x: An attenuated pathogen is alive and can multiply; a healthy immune system controls it, but in an immunocompromised person it may cause illness. Killed and subunit vaccines cannot multiply, so they do not carry this risk.

q: A major safety advantage of a subunit (recombinant protein) vaccine is that it:
o: Cannot cause the disease, as it contains no complete pathogen
Multiplies in the body and gives lifelong immunity in one dose
Contains the pathogen's whole genome in a weakened form
Gives immunity without the immune system taking part
x: A subunit vaccine contains only one or a few purified proteins of the pathogen, with no living organism or complete genetic material. It therefore cannot cause infection, though boosters may be needed.

q: To prepare a killed (inactivated) vaccine, the disease-causing organisms are:
o: Grown repeatedly in culture until they lose virulence but stay alive
Used only as a source of one gene, which is expressed in yeast
Treated with heat or chemicals so they cannot multiply but keep their antigens
Mixed with antibodies taken from an immunised animal
x: Killed vaccines, such as the Salk polio vaccine, use whole organisms treated with heat or chemicals like formaldehyde, so they cannot reproduce yet still stimulate antibody production. Weakening organisms while keeping them alive gives an attenuated vaccine instead.

q: In genetic engineering, restriction enzymes are used to:
o: Join DNA fragments together
Copy mRNA into DNA
Separate DNA fragments by size
Cut DNA at specific base sequences
x: Restriction endonucleases recognise particular short base sequences and cut the DNA there. Joining fragments is the job of DNA ligase.

q: In nature, bacteria produce restriction enzymes to:
o: Repair breaks in their own chromosome
Copy their plasmids before cell division
Destroy the DNA of invading bacteriophages
Digest proteins taken from their surroundings
x: Restriction enzymes cut foreign DNA such as that of infecting phages, 'restricting' viral growth. The bacterium's own DNA is protected, usually by methylation of the recognition sites.

q: The role of DNA ligase in making recombinant DNA is to:
o: Cut the plasmid open at its recognition site
Unwind the double helix into single strands
Seal the sugar-phosphate backbone between joined DNA fragments
Make many copies of the inserted gene
x: After sticky ends pair up by hydrogen bonding, DNA ligase forms the missing phosphodiester bonds, joining the fragments permanently. Cutting is done by restriction enzymes.

q: 'Sticky ends' produced by some restriction enzymes are:
o: Blunt double-stranded ends with no unpaired bases
Regions of DNA coated with protein to stop cutting
Sequences of repeated adenine bases added by ligase
Short single-stranded overhangs that can pair with complementary ends
x: Enzymes such as EcoRI cut the two strands at staggered points, leaving short unpaired tails. Any fragment cut with the same enzyme has complementary tails, so the ends readily base-pair.

q: The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises and cuts which DNA sequence (written 5' to 3' on one strand)?
o: GGATCC
GAATTC
AAGCTT
GCATGC
x: EcoRI cuts at GAATTC, between G and A, leaving AATT sticky ends. GGATCC is the site of BamHI and AAGCTT that of HindIII.

q: Most restriction enzyme recognition sites are palindromic. This means that:
o: The sequence contains only adenine and thymine
The site is found only once in every genome
The sequence reads the same 5' to 3' on both strands
The sequence is copied in reverse by ligase
x: In a palindromic site such as GAATTC, the complementary strand read 5' to 3' is also GAATTC. This symmetry lets the enzyme cut both strands in matching positions.

q: A plasmid is best described as:
o: A protein coat that carries DNA into a bacterium
A segment of the main bacterial chromosome
A ribosome-bound RNA molecule found in bacteria
A small circular DNA molecule that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome
x: Plasmids are small, circular, extra-chromosomal DNA molecules with their own origin of replication. This makes them convenient vectors for carrying foreign genes.

q: A plasmid vector usually carries an antibiotic-resistance gene so that:
o: Bacteria that have taken up the plasmid can be selected
The inserted human gene is switched on
The plasmid can be cut by the restriction enzyme
The human protein is protected from digestion
x: When the bacteria are grown on a medium containing the antibiotic, only those carrying the plasmid survive. The resistance gene therefore acts as a marker for transformed cells.

q: In recombinant DNA technology, the main job of a vector is to:
o: Cut the donor DNA into fragments
Join two DNA fragments with phosphodiester bonds
Destroy host cells that have not taken up DNA
Carry the foreign gene into the host cell where it can be copied
x: A vector, such as a plasmid or a modified virus, transports the gene into the host and replicates there along with it. Cutting and joining are done by restriction enzymes and ligase.

q: Recombinant DNA is DNA that:
o: Has been copied many times by DNA polymerase
Is found naturally only in viruses
Has been damaged by radiation and repaired
Contains genes combined from two different sources
x: Recombinant DNA is made by joining DNA from different sources, for example a human gene inserted into a bacterial plasmid. Simply copying DNA does not make it recombinant.

q: The same restriction enzyme is used to cut both the plasmid and the donor DNA because:
o: It makes the plasmid resistant to antibiotics
It prevents the host from recognising foreign DNA
It is the only enzyme able to cut circular DNA
It produces matching sticky ends that can pair together
x: Cutting both with one enzyme gives complementary sticky ends, so the gene fits into the opened plasmid and ligase can seal it. Different enzymes would usually give ends that do not pair.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in producing a human protein in bacteria?
o: Isolate gene, cut gene and plasmid, join with ligase, insert into bacteria, grow bacteria
Insert gene into bacteria, isolate gene, join with ligase, cut plasmid, grow bacteria
Cut plasmid, grow bacteria, isolate gene, insert into bacteria, join with ligase
Join with ligase, isolate gene, cut gene and plasmid, grow bacteria, insert into bacteria
x: The gene is first isolated, then both gene and plasmid are cut with the same restriction enzyme and joined by ligase. The recombinant plasmid is put into bacteria, which are cultured to make the protein.

q: The uptake of a recombinant plasmid by a bacterial cell from its surroundings is called:
o: Transformation
Transcription
Transduction
Translation
x: Transformation is the uptake of naked DNA by a cell. Transduction is DNA transfer by a bacteriophage, while transcription and translation are stages of protein synthesis.

q: Bacteria such as E. coli are widely used as hosts for recombinant genes mainly because they:
o: Carry out every modification that human cells do
Multiply very rapidly in simple culture media
Lack ribosomes and so make no proteins of their own
Have a nucleus that protects foreign DNA
x: Bacteria divide every few minutes in cheap media, so a recombinant cell soon becomes a huge population making the product. They are prokaryotes with no nucleus, and they cannot make all the modifications human cells make.

q: Yeast is sometimes preferred to bacteria as a host for producing a human protein because yeast:
o: Has no cell wall, so products leak out easily
Contains no DNA of its own to interfere
Divides faster than any bacterium
Is a eukaryote and can process proteins more like human cells
x: Yeast is a eukaryotic fungus, so it can fold and modify proteins (for example adding sugar groups) in ways bacteria cannot. It does have a cell wall and its own DNA, and it grows more slowly than bacteria.

q: Besides plasmids, which of the following is commonly used as a vector to carry genes into cells?
o: Ribosomes
Modified viruses such as bacteriophages
Histone proteins
Golgi bodies
x: Viruses naturally inject their nucleic acid into host cells, so modified phages and other viruses serve as vectors. Ribosomes, histones and Golgi bodies cannot carry and replicate a gene.

q: In genetic engineering, gel electrophoresis is used to:
o: Join DNA fragments into a plasmid
Insert recombinant plasmids into bacteria
Convert mRNA into complementary DNA
Separate DNA fragments according to their size
x: DNA is negatively charged and moves through a gel towards the positive electrode; smaller fragments move faster and further. This sorts fragments by size, for example after cutting with restriction enzymes.

q: BCG, given to newborns in Pakistan's routine immunisation programme, is a live attenuated vaccine that protects against:
o: Polio
Measles
Hepatitis B
Tuberculosis
x: BCG (Bacille Calmette-Guérin) contains a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis and protects against tuberculosis. Polio, measles and hepatitis B each have their own separate vaccines.

q: Compared with a vaccine prepared from virus particles in donated human blood, the recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is:
o: More dangerous, as yeast proteins cause the disease
Unable to produce memory cells
Safer, as it carries no risk of transmitting infections in blood
Effective only when given by mouth
x: Early hepatitis B vaccine came from the plasma of infected people, with a small risk of carrying other blood-borne infections. The yeast-made surface protein contains no virus, and it can be produced in unlimited amounts.

q: The immunity that develops after a person receives a vaccine is:
o: Naturally acquired active immunity
Artificially acquired active immunity
Artificially acquired passive immunity
Naturally acquired passive immunity
x: The person's own immune system makes the antibodies, so it is active; it is caused by deliberate injection, so it is artificial. Receiving ready-made antibodies would be passive immunity.

q: Scientists insert the gene for one surface protein of a virus into yeast and purify the protein for use as a vaccine. Which statement about this vaccine is correct?
o: It is a live attenuated vaccine
It cannot multiply in the body, as it contains no viral genome
It gives passive immunity
It contains the whole virus killed by heat
x: This is a recombinant subunit vaccine: one purified viral protein, with no nucleic acid. It cannot replicate, yet the immune system recognises it and forms antibodies and memory cells, giving active immunity.

q: Removing or disabling the genes that make a pathogen harmful, while keeping it alive, is a modern way of producing:
o: A killed vaccine
A toxoid
An antiserum
An attenuated vaccine
x: A live pathogen that has lost its ability to cause disease is, by definition, attenuated. A killed vaccine contains dead organisms, and an antiserum contains ready-made antibodies.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a plasmid used as a cloning vector?
o: It has its own origin of replication
It is part of the main bacterial chromosome
It has a site that a restriction enzyme can cut
It carries a marker gene such as antibiotic resistance
x: A useful vector replicates independently, can be opened by a restriction enzyme and carries a marker gene. Plasmids are separate from the bacterial chromosome, not part of it.

q: Killed vaccines usually need more doses (boosters) than live attenuated vaccines because:
o: Killed organisms cannot multiply, so the antigen dose stays small
Killed organisms are more likely to cause the disease
Killed vaccines contain no antigens at all
The body forms no memory cells after killed vaccines
x: A live attenuated organism multiplies for a while, giving a large, prolonged antigen exposure. Killed organisms do not multiply, so repeated doses are needed to build strong immunity; memory cells still form.

q: A DNA probe is:
o: An enzyme that cuts DNA at specific sites
A short, labelled, single-stranded DNA that pairs with a specific target sequence
An antibody that attacks infected cells
A circular DNA molecule found in bacteria
x: A probe is a short single-stranded piece of DNA (or RNA) carrying a label. It base-pairs only with its complementary sequence, so it shows whether that sequence is present.

q: DNA probes are made detectable by labelling them with:
o: A restriction enzyme
A radioactive isotope or a fluorescent dye
An antibiotic-resistance gene
A heat-stable DNA polymerase
x: Probes are tagged with radioactive phosphorus (detected on X-ray film) or a fluorescent marker. After hybridisation, the label shows where the probe has bound.

q: A DNA probe must be single-stranded because:
o: Double-stranded DNA cannot carry a label
Single strands are more resistant to enzymes
It can then base-pair with the complementary target strand
Only single strands can be copied by PCR
x: A probe works by complementary base pairing. If it were double-stranded, its bases would already be paired with each other and could not pair with the target.

q: In the context of diagnosis, nucleic acid hybridisation means:
o: Fusion of a B lymphocyte with a myeloma cell
Joining of DNA fragments by ligase
Complementary base pairing between a probe and a target nucleic acid
Crossing two varieties of an organism
x: Hybridisation is the pairing of two complementary single strands, such as a labelled probe binding to target DNA or RNA. Fusion of a B cell and myeloma cell forms a hybridoma, a different process.

q: Before a DNA probe can be used to detect a gene in a sample of double-stranded DNA, the sample DNA must be:
o: Separated into single strands, for example by heating
Joined into a plasmid with ligase
Translated into protein
Treated with antibodies
x: The target DNA is denatured (by heat or alkali) so that its two strands separate. Only then can the single-stranded probe pair with its complementary sequence.

q: A DNA probe has the sequence 5'-AGCTTG-3'. To which target sequence will it hybridise?
o: 3'-TCGAAC-5'
3'-AGCTTG-5'
3'-TCGAAG-5'
3'-CTAGGT-5'
x: Pairing is A with T and G with C, and the strands run antiparallel. Opposite 5'-AGCTTG-3' lies 3'-TCGAAC-5'. The sequence ending in G mismatches at the last base.

q: DNA probes can be used in disease diagnosis to:
o: Produce large amounts of insulin
Make bacteria resistant to antibiotics
Replace a faulty gene in a patient's cells
Detect a specific viral or bacterial gene in a patient's sample
x: A probe complementary to a pathogen's gene binds only if that pathogen's DNA or RNA is present. Making insulin and replacing faulty genes are treatment uses, not diagnosis.

q: Nucleic acid probes can detect some viral infections earlier than tests that look for the patient's antibodies because probes:
o: Stimulate the patient to make antibodies faster
Kill the virus so its proteins can be counted
Detect the virus's own nucleic acid, which is present before antibodies form
Work only after the immune response has finished
x: Antibodies take days to weeks to appear after infection. A probe looks directly for viral DNA or RNA, which is present from the start, so it can give a positive result earlier.

q: PCR stands for:
o: Polymerase chain reaction
Protein chain replication
Plasmid copying reaction
Primer cloning recombination
x: PCR is the polymerase chain reaction, developed by Kary Mullis. It uses a DNA polymerase in repeated cycles to copy a chosen DNA segment.

q: The main purpose of PCR is to:
o: Cut DNA into fragments of known size
Make millions of copies of a selected piece of DNA
Join a gene into a plasmid
Translate a gene into its protein
x: PCR amplifies a tiny amount of DNA into a large quantity that can then be tested or analysed. Cutting and joining are done with restriction enzymes and ligase.

q: The DNA polymerase used in PCR is obtained from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in:
o: Hot springs
The human intestine
Deep-sea cold waters
Soil around plant roots
x: Thermus aquaticus lives in hot springs, so its DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase) is stable at high temperatures. This lets it survive the repeated heating steps of PCR.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in one cycle of PCR?
o: Annealing of primers, denaturation, extension
Extension, denaturation, annealing of primers
Denaturation, annealing of primers, extension
Denaturation, extension, annealing of primers
x: First the DNA is heated so the strands separate (denaturation). On cooling, primers bind to the single strands (annealing), then Taq polymerase builds new strands from the primers (extension).

q: Starting with a single double-stranded DNA molecule, how many double-stranded copies of the target are expected after 5 cycles of PCR?
x: Each cycle doubles the number of DNA molecules, so after n cycles there are 2 to the power n copies. Two to the power 5 is 32; 64 would need 6 cycles.

q: A heat-stable DNA polymerase is essential in PCR because:
o: DNA cannot be copied below body temperature
It cuts the DNA into fragments at high temperature
The reaction is heated repeatedly to separate DNA strands
It joins primers to the ends of the DNA
x: Each cycle heats the mixture to about 90-95 degrees Celsius. An ordinary polymerase would be destroyed, but Taq polymerase survives and can be used through many cycles.

q: In PCR, primers are:
o: Enzymes that separate the two DNA strands
Short single-stranded DNA pieces that bind on either side of the target region
Labelled antibodies that detect the copied DNA
Plasmids that carry the copied DNA into bacteria
x: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing strand. Primers bind to the ends of the target sequence and give the polymerase its starting point, so only the region between them is copied.

q: PCR is especially useful in forensic investigations because it can:
o: Amplify DNA from a very small sample such as a drop of blood or a hair root
Determine a person's blood group without DNA
Produce antibodies against the criminal's cells
Repair DNA that has been completely destroyed
x: Crime scenes often leave only traces of DNA. PCR multiplies this into enough DNA for analysis. It cannot recover DNA that is completely destroyed.

q: Monoclonal antibodies are:
o: A mixture of antibodies against many different antigens
Antibodies made by bacteria carrying a human gene
Antibodies that act only against viruses
Identical antibodies made by a single clone of cells, specific for one antigen
x: Monoclonal means from one clone: all the cells descend from one parent cell and make exactly the same antibody. A mixture from many clones would be polyclonal.

q: A hybridoma cell is formed by fusing:
o: Two myeloma cells from different mice
A T lymphocyte with a red blood cell
An antibody-producing B lymphocyte with a myeloma (cancer) cell
A bacterial cell with a yeast cell
x: The hybridoma combines a B lymphocyte, which makes one specific antibody, with a myeloma cell, which divides without limit. The fused cell does both.

q: In the hybridoma technique, a myeloma cell is used because it:
o: Produces the specific antibody needed
Recognises the antigen injected into the mouse
Is unable to divide, so it stays stable
Can divide indefinitely in culture
x: Normal B lymphocytes die after a short time in culture. Myeloma cells are cancerous and keep dividing, so fusing them gives hybridomas that can be grown in large numbers.

q: To make a monoclonal antibody against a particular antigen, the B lymphocytes are usually taken from:
o: The bone marrow of an untreated mouse
A culture of myeloma cells
The spleen of a mouse that has been injected with that antigen
A bacterial colony carrying the antigen gene
x: Injecting the antigen makes the mouse produce B cells against it, which collect in the spleen. Untreated mice would have few B cells specific for that antigen.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in producing monoclonal antibodies?
o: Fuse myeloma cells, inject antigen into mouse, collect spleen B cells, culture them, select hybridomas
Inject antigen into mouse, collect spleen B cells, fuse with myeloma cells, select and clone hybridomas, culture them
Collect spleen B cells, culture them, inject antigen into mouse, fuse with myeloma cells, select hybridomas
Inject antigen into mouse, fuse with myeloma cells, collect spleen B cells, culture them, select hybridomas
x: The mouse is first immunised, then its spleen B cells are fused with myeloma cells. Hybridomas making the wanted antibody are selected and cloned, then grown in culture to produce the antibody.

q: The hybridoma technique for producing monoclonal antibodies was developed in 1975 by:
o: Kohler and Milstein
Watson and Crick
Boyer and Cohen
Jenner and Pasteur
x: Georges Kohler and Cesar Milstein fused B cells with myeloma cells in 1975 and later shared a Nobel Prize. Boyer and Cohen made the first recombinant DNA; Watson and Crick described the DNA double helix.

q: Home pregnancy test kits use monoclonal antibodies to detect which substance in urine?
o: Luteinising hormone from the pituitary
Insulin
Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG)
Oxytocin
x: hCG appears in urine soon after the embryo implants. Monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG bind it and give a visible coloured line.

q: The hormone detected in pregnancy tests (hCG) is produced by:
o: The anterior pituitary gland
The developing embryo and placenta
The corpus luteum
The ovarian follicle
x: hCG is made by the outer cells of the embryo that form part of the placenta. It keeps the corpus luteum active; the corpus luteum itself makes progesterone, not hCG.

q: Monoclonal antibodies help to locate tumours in the body because they:
o: Are made by the cancer cells themselves
Bind equally to all cells of the body
Bind specifically to antigens on cancer cells and can carry a detectable label
Make cancer cells divide faster so they show up
x: Antibodies against a tumour-specific antigen attach only to cancer cells. If they are tagged with a radioactive or fluorescent marker, scanning shows where the tumour and its spread are.

q: A pregnancy test strip shows the control line but no test line. The correct interpretation is that:
o: hCG was present but the antibodies were faulty
The test worked, but hCG was not detected in the urine
The test failed and gives no information
hCG was present in very large amounts
x: The control line shows that the urine flowed and the antibodies worked. The test line forms only when hCG is bound by the monoclonal antibodies, so its absence means hCG was not detected.

q: Monoclonal antibodies can be used in the laboratory diagnosis of an infection because they:
o: Make copies of the pathogen's DNA
Kill all the bacteria in the sample
Cut the pathogen's DNA at specific sites
Bind only to a specific antigen of the pathogen in a patient's sample
x: Each monoclonal antibody recognises one specific antigen, so a positive binding shows that the particular pathogen is present. Copying DNA is done by PCR, and cutting by restriction enzymes.

q: Monoclonal antibodies are preferred to antibodies collected from an animal's blood for diagnostic tests because they:
o: All recognise the same single antigenic site, so results are specific and consistent
Recognise many different antigens at the same time
Can be made without using any living cells
Remain active for ever without storage
x: Antibodies from blood are polyclonal: a mixture that may cross-react with other substances. Monoclonal antibodies are identical and bind one antigenic site, giving reliable, specific tests.

q: Which of the following is NOT a use of DNA probes?
o: Detecting a pathogen's genes in a blood sample
Producing human insulin in bacteria
Identifying people with a gene for a genetic disorder
Comparing DNA samples in forensic work
x: Probes are diagnostic tools that find specific DNA sequences. Producing insulin requires inserting the gene into bacteria and growing them, which is recombinant DNA production, not probing.

q: DNA fingerprinting, used to identify individuals, depends on the fact that:
o: All humans have exactly the same DNA sequence
DNA differs between the cells of one person
Only men have DNA patterns that can be compared
Each person, except identical twins, has a unique pattern of DNA sequences
x: Certain regions of DNA vary greatly between people, so the pattern of fragments is unique to each person except identical twins. Every cell of one person has the same DNA, which is why any tissue sample can be used.

q: Which statement correctly compares PCR and DNA probes in diagnosis?
o: PCR increases the amount of a DNA sequence, while a probe shows whether a sequence is present
PCR detects antibodies, while a probe detects antigens
Both PCR and probes cut DNA at specific recognition sites
A probe makes copies of DNA, while PCR labels it with dye
x: PCR amplifies a target sequence so there is enough to study. A labelled probe pairs with a complementary sequence and so identifies it. The two are often used together.

q: DNA probes can be used before birth or in adults to find carriers of an inherited disorder such as thalassaemia because they:
o: Correct the faulty allele in the cells
Measure the level of haemoglobin in the blood
Pair with the faulty allele's DNA sequence and reveal its presence
Prevent the faulty allele from being passed on
x: A probe complementary to the mutant allele binds only if that allele is present, so carriers and affected fetuses can be identified. Probes detect genes; they do not correct or block them.

q: Recombinant human insulin is produced on a large scale by inserting the human insulin gene into:
o: Pancreatic cells of pigs
Bacteria such as E. coli
Red blood cells of donors
Tobacco mosaic virus
x: The human insulin gene is placed in a plasmid and introduced into E. coli (or yeast), which then make human insulin. Before this, insulin came from the pancreases of slaughtered cattle and pigs.

q: An important advantage of recombinant human insulin over insulin extracted from cattle or pigs is that it:
o: Is identical to human insulin and less likely to cause allergic reactions
Has a different amino acid sequence that works faster
Can be taken by mouth instead of injected
Cures diabetes permanently after one course
x: Animal insulins differ from human insulin by one or a few amino acids and sometimes cause immune reactions. Recombinant insulin is identical to human insulin and can be made in unlimited amounts; it still has to be injected.

q: Insulin consists of two polypeptide chains. In one early method of making recombinant insulin:
o: Both chains were made by yeast and joined by DNA ligase
The two chains were made in separate bacterial cultures and then joined by disulphide bonds
Each chain was made by PCR and joined by hydrogen bonds
The chains were extracted from pig pancreas and joined in bacteria
x: The genes for the A-chain and the B-chain were put into separate batches of E. coli. The purified chains were then combined chemically, and disulphide bridges formed between them. Ligase joins DNA, not proteins.

q: Recombinant human growth hormone is used to treat children with:
o: Haemophilia
Diabetes mellitus
Anaemia caused by kidney failure
Pituitary dwarfism caused by lack of growth hormone
x: Children who make too little growth hormone grow very slowly and remain short. Injections of recombinant hGH help them grow. Haemophilia needs factor VIII, and kidney-failure anaemia needs erythropoietin.

q: Before it was made by genetic engineering, human growth hormone for treatment was obtained from:
o: Pancreases of cattle and pigs
Urine of pregnant women
Human blood plasma donations
Pituitary glands of dead human bodies
x: hGH was extracted from the pituitary glands of cadavers, giving only small amounts and a risk of passing on infections. Recombinant bacteria now give a safe, plentiful supply.

q: Interferons are produced naturally in the body by:
o: Red blood cells in the spleen
The beta cells of the pancreas
The anterior pituitary gland
Cells that have been infected by viruses
x: When a virus infects a cell, the cell releases interferons. These signal to nearby cells and help them resist the virus.

q: Recombinant interferon is used in the treatment of:
o: Viral hepatitis
Haemophilia
Pituitary dwarfism
Diabetes mellitus
x: Interferons interfere with viral replication, so they are used against viral infections such as hepatitis B or hepatitis C, and against some cancers. The other conditions need factor VIII, growth hormone and insulin.

q: Interleukins are proteins that mainly act as:
o: Enzymes that dissolve blood clots
Hormones that control blood glucose
Clotting factors that stop bleeding
Chemical messengers between white blood cells in the immune response
x: Interleukins are signals made by white blood cells (leucocytes) that regulate other white blood cells, for example stimulating lymphocytes to multiply. Clot dissolving is done by tPA, and glucose control by insulin.

q: Recombinant clotting factor VIII is given to patients suffering from:
o: Haemophilia
Sickle-cell anaemia
Diabetes insipidus
Dwarfism
x: In the commonest form of haemophilia the blood lacks working factor VIII, so it clots very slowly. Injections of factor VIII restore clotting.

q: The main advantage of recombinant factor VIII over factor VIII purified from donated blood is that it:
o: Works permanently after a single injection
Is a different protein that works better than the human one
Carries no risk of transmitting blood-borne viruses such as HIV
Can cure haemophilia by changing the patient's genes
x: Factor VIII from pooled blood donations infected many haemophiliacs with HIV and hepatitis viruses in the past. Recombinant factor VIII is made by cultured cells and avoids this risk, but injections are still needed regularly.

q: Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is used to:
o: Dissolve blood clots, for example in a heart attack
Speed up blood clotting in haemophilia
Increase red blood cell production
Lower blood glucose in diabetes
x: tPA breaks down clots blocking arteries, so it is given soon after a heart attack or a clot-caused stroke. Speeding clotting is the opposite effect, the role of factor VIII.

q: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) dissolves a blood clot by:
o: Converting fibrinogen into fibrin
Converting plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks down fibrin
Activating factor VIII
Destroying platelets in the blood
x: tPA activates plasminogen to the enzyme plasmin, which digests the fibrin threads holding the clot together. Converting fibrinogen to fibrin is done by thrombin and forms clots rather than dissolving them.

q: The hormone erythropoietin stimulates the production of:
o: White blood cells
Red blood cells
Platelets
Antibodies
x: Erythropoietin (EPO) acts on the bone marrow to increase the formation of red blood cells (erythrocytes), as its name suggests.

q: Patients with chronic kidney failure often need recombinant erythropoietin because:
o: The kidneys are the main site of erythropoietin production, so they become anaemic
Kidney failure destroys the bone marrow directly
Erythropoietin filters waste from the blood
Kidney failure causes too many red blood cells
x: Erythropoietin is made mainly by the kidneys. When they fail, little EPO is produced, red cell formation falls and the patient becomes anaemic. Recombinant EPO corrects this.

q: Gene therapy can be defined as:
o: Using antibodies to destroy cells carrying a faulty gene
Copying a faulty gene many times by PCR
Inserting a normal functional gene into a patient's cells to treat a genetic disorder
Giving a patient the protein that a faulty gene fails to make
x: Gene therapy treats the cause of a genetic disease by supplying working copies of the gene to the patient's cells. Giving the missing protein (such as insulin or factor VIII) is replacement therapy, not gene therapy.

q: A child is born with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) because of a faulty gene for the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). In the first approved gene therapy (1990), doctors:
o: Injected monoclonal antibodies against the faulty enzyme
Inserted normal ADA genes into the child's white blood cells and returned them to her
Gave a vaccine made of the ADA protein
Removed the faulty gene from every cell using restriction enzymes
x: White blood cells (T lymphocytes) were taken out, given a normal ADA gene by a modified virus, and returned to the patient. They then made the missing enzyme and immunity improved. Removing a gene from every cell is not possible.

q: In gene therapy, a normal gene is commonly carried into a patient's cells by:
o: Modified harmless viruses or liposomes
Restriction enzymes
Monoclonal antibodies
DNA ligase
x: Viruses naturally deliver nucleic acid into cells, so disabled viruses (such as retroviruses or adenoviruses) are used as vectors; fat droplets called liposomes can also carry DNA. Enzymes and antibodies cannot deliver genes.

q: Which statement about somatic gene therapy is correct?
o: The corrected gene is inserted into eggs or sperm
It changes every cell of the patient's body permanently
The corrected gene is not passed on to the patient's children
It can be done only on an early embryo
x: Somatic gene therapy modifies body cells, such as blood or lung cells, so the change is not inherited. Changing eggs, sperm or early embryos would be germ-line therapy, which could be passed on.

q: In trials of gene therapy for cystic fibrosis, normal genes were delivered to the cells lining the airways by:
o: An injection into the pancreas
An aerosol spray inhaled into the lungs
A pill swallowed with food
Transplanting new bone marrow
x: Cystic fibrosis mainly damages the lungs, so the normal gene, packed in liposomes or a modified virus, was inhaled to reach the airway lining. The effect lasted only a short time because these cells are replaced.

q: Which pair of recombinant product and its use is INCORRECT?
o: Insulin: treatment of diabetes mellitus
Factor VIII: treatment of haemophilia
Interferon: treatment of haemophilia
Human growth hormone: treatment of dwarfism
x: Interferons are antiviral proteins used against conditions such as viral hepatitis, not haemophilia. Haemophilia is treated with factor VIII, so that pairing is correct.

q: Which of the following correctly pairs a recombinant product with its use?
o: Tissue plasminogen activator: haemophilia
Erythropoietin: anaemia in kidney failure
Insulin: pituitary dwarfism
Factor VIII: dissolving clots in a heart attack
x: Erythropoietin increases red blood cell production in anaemia caused by kidney failure. tPA dissolves clots, the opposite of what a haemophiliac needs, and factor VIII promotes clotting.

q: Human growth hormone, now made by recombinant bacteria, is normally secreted in the body by the:
o: Anterior pituitary gland
Thyroid gland
Adrenal cortex
Pancreas
x: Growth hormone (somatotrophin) is secreted by the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland. The pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon, and the thyroid secretes thyroxine.

q: Before genetic engineering, interferons were scarce and expensive mainly because they:
o: Were made only by bacteria growing in hot springs
Lost activity immediately after being made
Could be extracted only in tiny amounts from human blood cells
Were obtained from the pancreases of pigs
x: Human interferon had to be purified from donated white blood cells, giving very small yields. Inserting interferon genes into bacteria made large-scale, cheaper production possible.

q: For producing human insulin in bacteria, scientists use DNA made from insulin mRNA rather than the gene taken directly from chromosomes, because:
o: Bacteria cannot remove the introns present in the chromosomal gene
Chromosomal DNA cannot be cut by restriction enzymes
mRNA-derived DNA is double the size of the gene
Bacteria cannot read DNA taken from any human cell
x: Human genes contain introns, which are removed from the mRNA in human cells. Bacteria have no machinery to remove introns, so complementary DNA made from mRNA by reverse transcriptase is used.

q: Which of the following is a recognised difficulty of gene therapy?
o: The inserted gene always passes to all future generations
Normal genes cannot be cut out or copied
The effect may be short-lived and the viral vector may trigger an immune reaction
Patients must avoid all proteins after treatment
x: Treated cells may die and be replaced, so repeated treatment can be needed, and the body may attack viral vectors. Somatic gene therapy does not affect future generations.

q: Interferons help to protect the body against viruses by:
o: Directly dissolving the virus's protein coat
Binding to viral DNA as a probe
Making neighbouring cells resistant to viral replication
Acting as antibodies made by plasma cells
x: Interferons released from infected cells bind to nearby cells and switch on defences that block viral multiplication. They are not antibodies and do not dissolve viruses directly.

q: Which of the following products obtained by biotechnology is NOT a hormone?
o: Insulin
Human growth hormone
Interferon
Erythropoietin
x: Insulin, growth hormone and erythropoietin are all hormones carried in the blood to target organs. Interferons are antiviral signalling proteins of the immune system, not hormones.

q: Haemophilia A, which is treated with recombinant factor VIII, is inherited as:
o: An autosomal dominant disorder
A Y-linked disorder
An autosomal recessive disorder
An X-linked recessive disorder
x: The gene for factor VIII is on the X chromosome, and the faulty allele is recessive. This is why haemophilia is far more common in males, who have only one X chromosome.

q: In ex vivo gene therapy:
o: Cells are removed from the patient, given the normal gene in the laboratory and returned
The normal gene is sprayed directly into the patient's lungs
The faulty protein is removed from the patient's blood
The gene is inserted into the patient's sperm or egg cells
x: Ex vivo means outside the living body: target cells such as white blood cells are modified in culture and put back. Delivering genes directly into the body, for example by aerosol, is in vivo therapy.

q: Recombinant interleukin-2 is used to boost immunity, for example in some cancers, because it stimulates:
o: Production of red blood cells
Multiplication of T lymphocytes
Formation of fibrin clots
Secretion of insulin
x: Interleukin-2 is a growth signal for T lymphocytes, increasing their numbers and activity against cancer cells. Red cell production is stimulated by erythropoietin.

q: In the name of the clot-dissolving drug tPA, the letters stand for:
o: Thrombin protein antagonist
Total platelet antibody
Tissue plasminogen activator
Thymus peptide activator
x: tPA is tissue plasminogen activator, a protein made naturally by blood vessel lining cells and now produced by recombinant DNA technology to dissolve clots.
